#8135. Continental Divide Trail Southern Terminus Monument to Be Relocated Due to Border Wall

A section of steel wall along the U.S.—Mexico border (Photo: PATRICK T. FALLON / Contributor via Getty)

Hikers can once again access the southern terminus of the Continental Divide Trail, more than two weeks after border wall construction closed down the southernmost 1.1 miles of the trail, the Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) says. But with the official end of the route now trapped between two sections of steel barrier, the obelisk that marks the terminus will need to be moved.

The southern mile of the trail had been closed since late October, when crews began widening the road that runs along the border fence and installing a second length of wall. Since 2025, that stretch has fallen inside the Fort Huachuca New Mexico National Defense Area, created when the Trump administration transferred 110,000 acres administered by the Bureau of Land Management to military control.

On Friday, the CDTC said it had received confirmation that hikers would once again be able to access the terminus. As before the closure, anyone entering the NDA needs to apply online for a permit from Fort Huachuca and undergo a background check; additionally, hikers who aren’t U.S. citizens need to be chaperoned by a permitted hiker who is.

“This closure came at a critical time for southbound hikers,” the CDTC said in a statement. “Completing the 3,100-mile trail is a monumental achievement, and the construction activities at the border created dynamic changes to the permitted NDA access in place during the past year.”

However, the construction has created a new issue: The Crazy Cook monument—the stone obelisk that marks the official end of the Continental Divide—is now sandwiched between the two steel barriers that make up the under-construction border wall. In an email, Audra Labert, the CDTC’s director of communications, said that while the organization had received reports that hikers had still been able to reach the monument by passing through the construction area, that arrangement is likely temporary.

“Authorities are now confirming plans to move the obelisk outside of the barrier walls for hikers to access, and passages between the barriers will eventually close,” Labert wrote. While it’s not clear when that could happen, the CDTC warned that the government would likely close the terminus to hikers again while it relocated the monument.

Construction on the border wall has complicated thru-hikers’ ability to access the southern termini of several long trails over the past year. In addition to the CDT, the federal government permanently closed access to the Arizona Trail’s southern terminus last November, a move that Matthew Nelson, the executive director of the Arizona Trail Association told Backpacker was “nothing less than a desecration.” In addition, authorities briefly banned Pacific Crest Trail hikers from touching the border wall this spring before abruptly reversing course. The under-construction barrier continues to figure in access and conservation fights along the southern border, with the Supreme Court recently ruling that the administration could continue construction of a new stretch of wall in Big Bend National Park.

#8134. 11 Climber Gift Ideas You Probably Haven’t Thought of Yet, According to Editors

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong)

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

Some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your new boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

Originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

It’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk showed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

Luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk

For climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. Those are only available at the museum, so if you’re not currently near Mariposa, California, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

The new Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

The Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the new film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

The oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

Note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a new collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

#8133. Astronaut Christina Koch Made History on Artemis II. But She Still Loves to Sleep in a Tent.

Christina making coffee while camping at Big Bend (Photo: Abigail Wise)

“WE ARE VERY close to being able to see Carroll Crater!” Christina Koch shouts across the campground, glancing up from her moonscope.

The NASA astronaut is bent over a small tube that looks like a telescope, attached to a tripod. A nearly full moon illuminates her curly hair, with her tent and a field of scraggly creosote bush behind her. The Big Bend National Park campsite is large enough to sleep eight people, but it’s just the two of us here tonight. Even at 10 P.M., the temperature hovers in the mid-70s. It’s already past my bedtime, but Koch and I came to the park to witness what happens in the sky after dark.

“If you look to the lower left, there’s a dark spot, almost like a mole. Carroll Crater is a little up to the left of that,” Koch says as I bend down to look through the lens, the dark splotches of the moon suddenly massive and detailed to my right eye.

Koch and the other three astronauts on the 2026 Artemis II mission named Carroll Crater after colleague and mission commander Reid Wiseman’s late wife. Mission specialist Koch, Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen made history in April 2026 when they completed a ten-day-long mission around the moon, traveling a record-setting 252,757 miles from Earth, livestreaming the event, and going viral along the way. It made Koch the first woman to travel around the moon, adding another record to her list, which also includes the longest spaceflight by a woman (328 days throughout 2019 and 2020), and embarking on the first all-women spacewalk on October 18, 2019.

FIVE MONTHS AFTER the Artemis II crew touched down in the Pacific Ocean, Koch and I met in Big Bend to go on our own small mission: nighttime photography. Last night, September 26, was a full moon, and it still looks massive, bright, and round above the Chihuahuan Desert tonight. The only way you can tell it’s no longer full, Koch tells me, is that you can spot a little bit of the Terminator in the upper right corner. The Terminator, the line that divides the side of the moon that’s glowing from the one going into shadow, looks like a sliver of darkness that shifts the moon’s craters into 3D.

“Imagine seeing that when it’s literally this big in your view,” Koch says, holding her hands wide.

We’ve spent the evening on a couple-mile hike and scramble up to Balanced Rock to photograph the stars and moon. Balanced Rock is a massive boulder suspended between stacks of rocks on either side so that it appears to hover above the ground. Sitting next to the boulders, Koch set up her tripod and snapped shots of the massive, orange moon rising and the stars sparkling above the syenite rock formations. She even managed to capture the shooting star we both spotted streaking above.

Photography is her hobby, she tells me. She’s been taking pictures since she did so for her college paper at North Carolina State University, from which she holds multiple degrees in physics and electrical engineering.

Her love of photography came in handy for her space missions. NASA, which features an entire photography training team, worked with Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew ahead of their historic trip to optimize documenting photos of the moon and Earth from space. They had to learn how to use a wide lens as the Artemis II crew occupied a very small vehicle, how to use the proper f-stop and shutter speeds, and how to take more technical photography, too, to report back on anything that appeared broken and other details for the on-the-ground engineers.

Photography wasn’t the only arts-based training the Artemis II crew took on prior to their mission. The four astronauts decided to seek out and collaborate with a poet to assist them in better describing what they saw in space. Koch still trains with the poet today. “He helps me a lot with metaphors and language, but also just seeing the beauty in things,” she says.

The crew’s holistic approach is, in many ways, different from how older generations of astronauts prepared for space travel. The Apollo Generation, which included astronauts like Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, who became the first people to walk on the moon in 1969, focused on thousands of hours of moonwalk and lunar surface simulations and reduced gravity training. While practical, technical skills were vital to the Artemis II astronauts, too, they also concentrated heavily on team dynamics: the crew embarked on a National Outdoor Leadership School (NOLS) trip together, a common practice today for NASA teams. “We made so many commitments to being a crew that loved and trusted each other,” says Koch. “NOLS was one of the things that we did when we learned a lot of those actual skills to keep us in a good place and keep us friends.”

Another focal point for the Artemis II crew was learning about the meaning behind their destination. “We worked with cultural experts on the moon and tried to cultivate a deeper understanding of the many facets of where we were going, not just the scientific ones,” says Koch.

But for the differences in training approaches and communication styles throughout history, the narrative around space exploration has, in many ways, remained the same. “Beautiful concepts like love and peace, and going for all of humanity, those have always been a part of it,” says Koch. “There is almost no one who went [to space] and didn’t have beautiful things to say.”

AFTER A COUPLE of hours taking pictures near Balanced Rock, Koch and I are back at camp, eating dinner under the moonlight. She’s cooked up some simple couscous on a backpacking stove and finishes it with a handful of pine nuts.

“This is how low-key I am,” says Koch, gesturing to her pot. “It’s practically plain couscous, and I’m so excited for it because I was such a dirtbag backpacker for so long. This is very standard and kind of nostalgic.”

Over the years, Koch, who’s 47 years old, has developed an arsenal of dirtbag and outdoors skills. She’s an accomplished climber—mostly sport, trad, and ice—and skis both downhill and cross-country. Despite growing up near the ocean in North Carolina, where her dad taught Koch and her four siblings how to sail, she didn’t begin surfing until her mid-thirties; now it’s one of her favorite sports. She also loves trail running, but after struggling with hip dysplasia for years (the trip to Big Bend was a few months after she had a hip replacement), Koch took up triathlons instead to balance out the running with cycling and swimming. In order to do so, she had to learn to swim distances, which she tackled in her mid-forties. “It took me like two years to learn to swim. I’m very uncoordinated,” Koch insists.

One of Koch’s biggest adventures, outside of the Artemis II mission, took place in 2006 when she and some friends climbed Mount Kenya. The group ascended the 17,058-foot mountain, which requires technical climbing to reach the highest summits, without a porter. The first night camping on the trip, Koch opened the door of her tent after hearing a strange noise; a sea of glowing eyes reflected back at her as a herd of wild buffalo passed by. “I was like, ‘We’re going to get trampled and die,’” she says.

Luckily, the herd moved on without incident, but Koch had another problem: she quickly realized that she hadn’t packed enough food for the ascent. That same night, a ranger came by and had cut his finger very badly but didn’t have a way to sew up his wound. Koch and her friends had a first-aid kit on hand and helped patch up his injury in exchange for a can of beans.

The beans, along with the food she did pack, helped fuel her through the week-long backpacking trip, in which she and her friends carried a lot of weight, hauling their climbing gear up to the technical section of the mountain. While they didn’t make it all the way to the summit they were targeting, they did climb for a stretch of it. “We made it higher than you could walk up,” says Koch.

Coming off the mountain, though, the climbers were out of food and cash, and rather than hike another eight miles, they managed to scrounge together their very last coins to ride a bus back to town. “I must have lost so much weight,” she says. “My pants were hanging off of me, and we were very hungry.”

But they arrived at their target hotel safely and used their credit cards to book a room. “I will never forget the next morning we were eating at an all-you-can-eat breakfast buffet,” says Koch. “It was the funniest dichotomy of going from really feeling like we were at the end of our line, coasting out on fumes, to being completely OK and in the borderline lap of luxury. It was just so ridiculous.”

Professionally, Koch spent several years of her early career traveling to remote, isolated landscapes, conducting scientific research. She always wanted to be an astronaut, but wasn’t interested in pursuing the typical paths astronauts often follow, such as obtaining a degree in aerospace engineering or getting a pilot’s license. “I want to be in nature, not flying over it, so that was just never a hobby that really called my name,” she says.

So while Koch has dreamed of being an astronaut since she was a child, she wasn’t going to give up her interests to pursue some kind of checklist to become one. Instead, she followed her passions for science and nature into often harsh environments. She worked as a research associate for Raytheon Polar Services, stationed in Antarctica, where the area closes down for months at a time due to extreme cold and darkness. “There’s no mail, no fresh food, no people in or out for eight months,” Koch says. “That was something I went and did when I was 25.”

She also worked as an electronics and instrument technician in Greenland, Alaska, and again in Antarctica before traveling to American Samoa in 2012 as a station chief for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). It was there, while stationed in American Samoa, that she met her husband, Bob Koch, who at the time was working as a GIS coordinator.

During a time before smartphones and internet access were a given, Bob quickly figured out that Koch drove by a favorite surf break of his 45 minutes east of where he lived on her way to work each morning. So Bob asked Koch to take a photo of the surf on her commute, and then send it to him over the reliable internet at her laboratory. “She was my surf report buddy, and then obviously things took off from there,“ says Bob, who now works for the Army Corps of Engineers. “We called it Peter Pan Island.”

Not long after meeting, Koch decided to apply to become an astronaut, and when she was accepted in 2013, she and Bob moved to Houston, Texas, where NASA’s Johnson Space Center is based and where the couple now lives with their dog, Sadie. “Going from a full-on dirtbag lifestyle to the most regimented, military-like astronaut training, with these requirements and proficiencies, was like whiplash for me,” says Koch, who used to view more conventional career paths as selling out or growing up. “Everything I did was towards free time and the outdoors and very minimal requirements in life.”

But her thinking soon shifted as she embraced her new job. “I used to think that all of these people working really hard don’t know what life is really about,” she says. “And then I realized, actually, maybe it’s totally OK to work really hard for something and make a difference.”

WHEN ARTEMIS II launched into space from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, the four crewmembers had prepared themselves, each other, and their loved ones for the risks and reality of the adventure they were undertaking. In preparation, the Kochs bought a Sprinter van.

“[Bob] was trying to figure out what do you do when your wife goes to the moon?” says Koch. “You can’t go to work; you’re not going to be able to concentrate. If you’re sitting at home, you’re going to be worried. So he organized a road trip with his friends.”

Bob devised a plan: Mission Break 80, in which he and his friends would golf and surf their way from Florida, where Artemis II launched, to San Diego, where the crew was set to land. They’d camp along the way in his new van, which proudly displayed an Artemis II magnet. As a joke, Bob created Mission Break 80 patches to match. And while he only made it as far as Houston in the van, the distraction largely worked.

“Going surfing every morning took me away from my phone for two hours, or the act of setting up camp and being outside just created a calming effect,” says Bob. “That was my way of coping with the mission: actually spending time outdoors, away from devices, but just close enough in case I needed to get a call.”

Bob got two half-hour calls with Koch during the mission, one on day three and the next on day seven. He took the first call from the beach with wet hair and waves in the background.

One thing the crew and their families had not prepared for was how many people would watch the Artemis II mission worldwide. “Moon joy,” the excitement of the 2026 orbit, as it was dubbed, went viral. NASA reported more than 149.4 million views of the launch, splashdown, and lunar flyby on its own platforms alone. An estimated 400,000 people gathered in person to watch the launch in Florida, according to Smithsonian Magazine. “They kind of caught lightning in a bottle,” says Bob. “I think it was a combination of the synergy of the crew collectively and all their unique personalities and kind of how they played off each other. And I think it was just some timing where people really wanted a positive story that they could follow and all rally around.”

While #moonjoy was trending on every social platform, Koch and the rest of the Artemis II crew were oblivious to the buzz on the ground. “We never dreamed it would become what it was,” says Koch. “We actually might never know what happened on Earth while we were gone,” she continues. “Earth had a party for us, and we weren’t there.”

On the second of their two allotted calls, Bob realized he had to let Koch know how popular the mission had become. He told his wife that she and her colleagues were inspiring people down on Earth. “I told her how proud I was and how inspirational she and the crew and mission were,” he says. “I remember she teared up.”

Koch remembers the call vividly, too. “He was like, ‘Tina, I need to tell you something. Something is happening down here. You guys are having an impact. You’re moving the needle,’” she recalls.

“It’s funny because when you cry in space, your tears well up in your eyes, and they just stay there,” says Koch, explaining that the lack of gravity makes it so that tears don’t fall. “I was wiping my buoyant tears, and I was like, ‘That’s all we ever wanted…’ When we designed our mission patch, it was ‘A II;’ we made it look like the word ‘all.’ That was our goal: for all.”

IT’S NEARLY NOON and the sun is blazing in Balmorhea, Texas. Koch and I just met up to cool off in the world’s largest spring-fed swimming pool, a 1.3-acre body of brisk water in the high desert of West Texas. We’re taking a dip with the locals—kids splashing and shrieking with delight, groups of women floating on inner tubes, and a handful of scuba divers—before driving out into the 91-degree desert to hike and camp.

As we chat and tread water, I glance down to see schools of fish darting around our legs. “Sometimes they bite,” Koch told me earlier, “which is kind of fun!”

If I look long enough, with a little luck, I might even see a turtle, one frequent swimmer mentioned when I arrived. Koch says she spotted them last time she was here on a van trip.

“I’m going to go do some laps and look for turtles,” she tells me, snapping on her goggles and doing the breaststroke over toward the deep end, which reaches 25 feet.

I follow her, trailing behind, gazing into the sparkling, royal blue water. Behind me, a group of teens is taking turns launching off a diving board, and a small family is gearing up to scuba dive. We’ll need to head out soon if we want to snag a camping permit before the park’s visitor center closes. Koch knows it’s time to get going, too.

“I’m just going to jump off of the high dive one time before we go,” she announces, making her way to the opposite side of the pool. As I watch, she climbs out and walks briskly to the edge. She hesitates briefly as she eyes the water below. Then, she jumps, suspended in space for just a moment before she splashes back down to Earth.

Abigail Wise is the brand director at Outside. She’s been fascinated with space since her mom sent her to a science space camp one summer in elementary school. These days, she’s been known to drag her own kids out to watch meteor showers in the middle of December near their home in northern New Mexico—and insists it’s worth every whine.

This article is from the Winter 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

#8132. Rodents Keep Destroying Your Hiking Gear? Here’s How to Keep It Safe

A chipmunk chews its way into a hiker's backpack. (Photo: Stanislav Sablin/Getty Images)

One of my favorite parts of being outdoors is the wildlife, and that includes rodents. I love watching squirrels chase each other around tree trunks, and I may or may not have had a “pet” chipmunk in one of my cabins during a horseback guiding season. I talk to marmots when I’m alone, and hearing the chirp of a pika makes my day. But I draw the line at the little buggers crawling over my face in a shelter, chewing through my trekking pole straps, or getting into my food bag.

This is a common occurrence in the backcountry, whether you’re hiking a populated trail or posted up at some far-flung campsite. While no one I know has a perfect mouse-proofing strategy, here are a few tips and tricks to help keep rodents at bay and protect your pack pockets, straps, and food.

The most vulnerable parts of your gear are the deliciously salty pack straps, trekking pole straps, and pockets where you’ve forgotten you left food. While keeping your straps clean is easier said than done after days of sweaty hiking, reducing the tantalizing salty odors will work wonders in keeping sodium-fiending rodents away. If you can, dunk your straps in running water a few times throughout the day, and especially at night when you get to camp.

You can also drip a few drops of hand sanitizer onto trekking pole straps to make them less appealing, and tucking a dryer sheet into salty pockets or around hammock straps can also work as a rodent deterrent. Finally, always stash your trekking poles upright in the ground to keep the straps less accessible.

The bear hang is a time-honored backcountry art form, but if you’ve ever seen an acrobatic mouse shimmy down the rope and land a perfect 10 on your backpack, you know this protective measure doesn’t translate perfectly to rodent-proofing. The solution, as many of us have seen in high-traffic trail shelters, is something I call the Mouse Swing. This is simply your standard piece of paracord or bear-hang rope, but with a barrier tied in the middle.

I’ve used everything from a (clean!!) tuna can to a quart-size yogurt container lid. Punch a hole in the can or plastic lid, run your string through the hole with knots to secure it in place, and you’ll have a lightweight, highly functional barrier between your pack and the string. Make sure your bag is a few feet above the ground or shelter floor to prevent high jumpers from making the leap.

Along with salty straps, mice, rats, and squirrels are highly attracted to food smells. The worst pocket destruction I encountered was when I carefully hung my pack from the rafters of a shelter but forgot to remove the remains of an energy bar from the pocket, and an industrious mouse chewed right through the material. Don’t forget to check your pockets for lip balm, energy gels, or the remains of your lunchtime protein bar.

While a hard-sided bear canister is the best protection against animals getting into your food supply, I prefer not to carry the bulky, heavy contraption unless it’s required in the area. The next best thing is the Ursack Allmitey, a heavy-duty food bag made from Spectra, a specialized material with one of the highest strength-to-weight ratios out there. Once tied properly closed, it’s next to impossible for critters to chew through or squeeze through the opening. If you’re in an area where rodents are the only concern, you can size down in bulk to the Ursack Minor, a Kevlar bag that isn’t tough enough to stand up to bears, but can keep smaller toothy critters at bay.

I’ve also used RatSacks for food drops in the desert. They’re heavier than the Ursack Minor, but have proven virtually indestructible against desert rodents, and some national parks like Canyonlands lend them out for free. These are made from stainless steel mesh with a heavy-duty Velcro closure at the top, and while they aren’t bearproof, I’ve never had a smaller animal bust through the dense metal mesh.

Finally, if scent control is your primary priority, you can further streamline your gear with LokSak OPSAK bags. These won’t prevent sharp little teeth from chewing through them, but the polyethylene material and secure zip tops are completely odorproof and can keep curious squirrels and chipmunks from testing them in the first place.

I hesitate to write this since it’s such a Big If, but if you’re camping somewhere that the risk of running into a bear is zero, you can bring smelly items into your tent. This isn’t foolproof—you run a risk of an unusually bold mouse chewing into your tent—but by and large, most small rodents will be deterred by your massive sleeping form and won’t bother trying to break in.

#8130. How Hillary Dawa Sherpa Survived 6 Days Alone on Mount Everest

On May 29, a Nepali high-altitude worker named Hillary Dawa Sherpa ran out of oxygen while descending Mount Everest at the edge of the Death Zone. Days went by, and officials assumed he was dead. And then, six days after vanishing, he crawled on his hands and knees out of the Khumbu Icefall toward Base Camp, where he was rescued by camp workers.

Hillary Dawa’s improbable story of survival ignited a debate about safety and ethics on the world’s highest peak. And the 57-year-old wasn’t supposed to have been on Everest’s highest slopes in the first place.

He was originally hired to work as a seasonal cook at the Camp II setup of low-cost Nepali guiding company Himalayan Traverse Adventures. The company had just two paying clients for the 2026 season: Chris Thrall, a British ex-Royal Marine, and Mariusz Chmielewski, a plumber from Poland.

But late in the expedition, Hillary Dawa was asked to guide Thrall up the mountain, after Himalayan Traverse Adventures sent one of its experienced climbing Sherpas home.

“I was only supposed to be a cook, but they offered me 10,000 Rupees a day to climb with the clients,” Hillary Dawa told Outside. “I didn’t even want to go to Everest this year.”

Outside reached out to Himalayan Traverse Adventures but did not receive answers for this story. Hillary Dawa said company management believed Thrall was incapable of making it above Camp IV. But Thrall eventually reached the summit. Hillary Dawa and Chmielewski turned back before the top and retreated to Camp IV. On the descent, the company’s other climbing Sherpa sped ahead down the peak, while Thrall, Chmielewski, and Hillary Dawa continued together. They were racing toward the May 29 closing date, which is when Sherpas would remove ladder bridges from the Khumbu Icefall.

“I was carrying eight empty oxygen tanks and the client’s sleeping bag,” Hillary Dawa said. “If I lost an oxygen bottle, they would deduct $250 from my salary, so I had to bring it all down.”

Eventually, he ran out of oxygen and sat down to rest, telling Thrall to continue. Thrall and Chmielewski reached Camp II at 23,000 feet and radioed for help, saying Hillary Dawa was in trouble. But Himalayan Traverse did not mount an immediate search and rescue mission.

Days went by with no sign of him. A larger company, 8K Expeditions, eventually launched a rescue. Assuming nobody could survive that long without food and water, reporters increased the season’s fatality rate to six. His family prepared funeral rites at a monastery in Kathmandu.

Meanwhile, high on the mountain, Hillary Dawa fought to live. After regaining consciousness, he inched down, stopping at abandoned tents to search for scraps of food and water. At the Khumbu Icefall, he found safety ropes buried under snow and ladder bridges intact. He was within sight of Base Camp when another disaster struck—a ladder bridge collapsed, sending him plunging 50 feet into a crevasse. He caught a safety rope, which saved his life.

“I looked down and saw a small ledge of snow,” he said. “I kept my head straight and slid down the rope and landed on the ledge. And that’s when my leg broke.”

Injured but alive, Hillary Dawa spent the next two and a half days on the precipice. He survived by eating a few pieces of candy and a packet of instant coffee, rationing the calories carefully and sucking on ice to moisten his mouth. On the night of June 3, his fifth day alone on Everest, an avalanche rumbled into the crevasse. Hillary Dawa braced for the worst.

“I thought about God,” he said. “I prayed: ‘Either let me die here or help me get out.’”

He lived. And in the morning, he saw that the slide had created a snow ramp to the surface. Using his good leg, Hillary Dawa pushed himself backward to the surface. Severely dehydrated and weak, he spent the next day and night crawling through the labyrinth of ice, eventually emerging near Base Camp. Within a few hours, Hillary Dawa became a global sensation.

While his ability to survive against seemingly impossible odds is the stuff of legend, his ordeal also raises uncomfortable questions about who bears the greatest risks on Everest, and what happens when expeditions cut corners.

#8129. Two Hikers Rescued from Wet Snow and Freezing Temperatures Deep in the White Mountains

A view west from Mount Bond in New Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness. (Photo: MikeCherim / Getty Images)

Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.

Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and currently partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain.

While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions.

Although they’d packed lights, food, and water, New Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) said the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry.

NHFG said that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th.

In the wake of the incident, New Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains.

This incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

#8125. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8122. First Look: The Amflow UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro

In the space of three years, Amflow has made a name for itself by designing versatile e-bikes that excel on mountain trails, gravel roads, and other routes that begin where the pavement ends. Now, it’s introducing a new pair of city-oriented e-bikes that exemplify the brand’s expertise in engineering, support, and safety. The UE Carbon and UE Carbon Pro might be Amflow’s first purpose-built commuter models, but they’re the culmination of everything the brand built since its inception.

Most riders spend their time in urban environments, so it makes sense that Amflow set out to design a bike that shines across the broad spectrum of daily use. The UE Carbon series builds on the brand’s history and is more than a mere concession to urban riders. This bike feels natural from the very first pedal, regardless of a rider’s size, riding style, or itinerary, and it’s tailor-made for commuting, running errands, heading on a fitness ride, and everything in between.

The foundation of the UE Carbon’s everyday adaptability is its rider-friendly design. The bike’s sleek carbon frame keeps its weight down; at 46 pounds, it’s nimble enough for navigating dense urban cores, as well as light enough for lifting onto public transport and into a storage space. A step-through design promotes an upright riding posture, which—combined with substantial adjustability and easy-to-maneuver 26-inch wheels—allows users of varying sizes to get in the saddle. The geometry also supports loads up to 44 pounds in the front and 59 pounds at the rear with the right accessories. The rear rack’s MIK HD compatibility adds quick-release modularity, letting the bike adapt to urban commuting, family outings, and light outdoor adventures.

From a technical perspective, the UE Carbon reaps the benefits of Amflow’s excellent array of components. Both the standard and Pro models feature the premium Avinox M2 motor, which provides 1,100W of peak power and 125 Nm of torque. The robust drive system cruises 30% inclines with ease, with a smooth overall feel and low noise output (approximately 45 dBA). Plus, with a maximum range of 82 miles via a 600Wh removable battery, the UE Carbon can go for multiple days without a recharge.

As with all Amflow bikes, there’s top-notch tech throughout. Both the UE Carbon and Carbon Pro include electronic shifting (the major difference between the two models is the drivetrain and its components: a 10-speed electronic rear derailleur and chain on the Carbon, while the Pro has a three-speed electronic internal geared hub and Gates drive belt). The 1.4-inch cockpit display grants intuitive control of the bike’s functions with a simple, clean interface, and riders can connect to an Apple Watch and the Avinox Ride app, which also includes a lost mode. Additionally, an integration with the Apple Find My lets users track the bike’s location in real time and activate its sound alert. An included frame and battery lock will hopefully ensure you never have to use the lost mode or tracking features.

That suite of features, plus the UE Carbon’s all-around functionality and ergonomic design, makes it the perfect choice for those who want a bike that can handle anything the city serves up. It’s a proud next step in Amflow’s expanded e-bike offerings and is bound to put the brand on even more riders’ radars.

Proudly born in 2023, Amflow is the creation of tech experts with a limitless passion for riding electric bikes. The company strives to amaze with an unmatched combination of power, range, and performance, hidden in sleek bike bodies. Amflow’s commitment to the e-bike industry is to make its bikes the go-to for all e-bike riders looking to turn any terrain into a wonderland of possibilities.

#8119. How to Make a Handprint Calendar

Hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

We love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

#8116. Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

As soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”

The sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential issues.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8113. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

Between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more important to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

Even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy says. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”

The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up says, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he says. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a new way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

For activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8111. 41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)

It’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

2. Plan a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”

40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8109. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”

This article was originally published on June 7, 2022
